The Claims Academy is not a physical building. It operates as a virtual training organization. All course materials, including this manual, are available on the company intranet under the Claims Training portal. Instructors are senior adjusters and managers who have completed the Trainer Certification course. If you have questions about a procedure in this manual, you should first consult your direct supervisor. If your supervisor is unable to answer, you may submit a question through the Claims Academy Help Desk.

1.2 Who Should Use This Manual

This manual is intended for all claims employees, including:

- Trainee adjusters who have completed their first week of orientation.
- Experienced adjusters who are moving into a new line of business (for example, from auto to property).
- Claims assistants and intake specialists who handle the initial report of loss.
- Supervisors and managers who are responsible for reviewing claim files for quality and compliance.
- Any employee who is new to Northgate Mutual and needs an overview of how the Claims Division operates.

If you are a trainee, you will receive a printed copy of this manual during your first day of training. You are expected to bring it to all classroom sessions and to your field training assignments. You will also have access to the electronic version, which is updated more frequently than the printed copy. The electronic version is the authoritative source. If there is a conflict between the printed manual and the electronic version, the electronic version controls.

1.3 How to Use This Manual

Each section of this manual covers one phase of the claim handling lifecycle. Sections are numbered and are designed to be read in order during your first two weeks of training. After that, you will use the manual as a reference tool. Cross-references to other sections are provided throughout. For example, when you are working on coverage determination, you will be directed to Section 4 for detailed guidelines and to Form C-101 for the coverage analysis worksheet.

At the end of most sections, you will find a list of related forms and a brief description of when each form is used. You are not expected to memorize every form number. Instead, you should become familiar with the Forms Index in Section 12 and learn to look up forms as needed.

The manual also contains a number of "Practice Pointers" that appear in shaded boxes. These are tips from experienced adjusters that are meant to help you avoid common mistakes. They are not formal policy, but they reflect the best practices that have been developed over years of claim handling.

1.4 The Claims Handling Lifecycle: A Brief Introduction

This manual follows the lifecycle of a claim from the initial report to final resolution. The lifecycle is divided into the following phases:

1. Initial Intake – The claim is reported, and basic information is collected.
2. Coverage Determination – The policy is reviewed to determine whether the loss is covered.
3. Investigation – Facts are gathered to establish liability and damages.
4. Evaluation – The claim is valued, and a settlement offer is considered.
5. Resolution – The claim is settled, denied, or litigated.

Not every claim goes through every phase in a straight line. For example, a claim may be reported, investigated, and then returned to coverage review when new facts emerge. You will learn to manage these changes as you gain experience. The important thing is to understand the purpose of each phase and the documentation that is required at each step.

1.5 The Role of the Claims Adjuster

As a claims adjuster, you are the face of Northgate Mutual to the policyholder and the claimant. Your job is to investigate the facts, apply the policy language, and make a fair and timely decision. You are also responsible for documenting your work so that another adjuster, a supervisor, or a court can understand what you did and why.

Good claim handling is built on three pillars:

- Timeliness – You must complete each step within the timeframes described in this manual and in your state's regulations.
- Accuracy – You must collect and record accurate information. Do not guess or assume. If you are unsure about a fact, ask.
- Fairness – You must treat every party with respect and make decisions based on the policy and the law, not on emotion or bias.
Your supervisor will work with you to create a training plan based on your job classification and your experience level. Course registration is handled through the Learning Management System (LMS). Course Number: A-204
Course Title: Advanced Auto Claims Handling
Course Length: 3 days (24 classroom hours)
Delivery: Instructor-led, in person at the Northgate Claims Academy training center; one session offered each quarter. A virtual option is available for adjusters located more than 100 miles from a training center.
Prerequisites: Successful completion of A-101 (Auto Claims Fundamentals) and A-102 (Property Damage Estimating) within the past 24 months. Adjusters with more than five years of continuous auto claim handling experience may request a waiver of the prerequisites from the Academy coordinator. Waiver requests must be submitted in writing and approved before registration.
Intended Audience: Claims adjusters, senior claim representatives, and claim examiners who handle auto claims involving complex coverage questions, multiple parties, or significant exposure. The course is also recommended for adjusters who are preparing for a promotion to a senior or examiner role.

Course Description

Advanced Auto Claims Handling is designed for adjusters who have mastered the fundamentals and now face the kinds of claims that do not fit neatly into the standard workflow. The course covers the following topics:

- Advanced coverage analysis, including the application of policy exclusions and endorsements in multi-vehicle accidents
- Handling claims involving uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage, including the coordination of benefits when more than one policy applies
- Investigation techniques for claims involving disputed liability, including the use of scene reconstruction reports and expert witnesses
- Evaluation of total loss vehicles, including the use of market valuation reports and the handling of diminished value claims
- Negotiation and settlement strategies for claims with multiple claimants or with claimants who are represented by counsel
- Documentation and file organization requirements for litigated claims

The course combines lecture, case study discussion, and small-group exercises. You will be asked to work through several realistic claim scenarios from initial intake to final resolution. The scenarios are based on actual claims handled by Northgate Mutual adjusters, with names and identifying details changed.

Chapter 1: Introduction and Training Requirements

1.1 Purpose of This Manual

This manual sets out the standardized procedures that Northgate Mutual claims professionals are expected to follow when handling automobile claims. It is used in Claims Academy courses and is also the day-to-day reference for adjusters in the field. The manual supports three goals: fair and prompt handling of claims, consistent application of coverage and policy provisions, and compliance with the laws and regulations of the states where Northgate Mutual does business.
## 1.2 Training Requirements

All new claims personnel must complete the Claims Academy Core Curriculum before they are assigned a claim file independently. The Core Curriculum consists of the following courses:

| Course Number | Course Title | Delivery Method | Hours |
|---------------|--------------|-----------------|-------|
| CA-101 | Introduction to Auto Claims | Classroom | 8 |
| CA-102 | Policy Reading and Coverage | Classroom | 16 |
| CA-103 | Claim Intake and Initial Contact | Classroom + Shadowing | 12 |
| CA-104 | Investigation Fundamentals | Classroom + Field | 24 |
| CA-105 | Evaluation and Negotiation | Classroom | 16 |
| CA-106 | Claim Resolution and Payment | Classroom | 8 |
| CA-107 | Fraud Awareness | Online | 4 |

New adjusters must complete CA-101 through CA-103 before handling intake calls or entering new claims into the system. CA-104 through CA-107 must be completed within the first six months of employment. Adjusters who do not complete the Core Curriculum within the required timeframe will have their claim assignment authority suspended until the courses are finished.

Annual continuing education (CE) requirements are set by each state where the adjuster is licensed. The Licensing and Compliance team tracks CE deadlines and will notify adjusters 90 days before any license renewal date. It is the adjuster's responsibility to confirm that CE credits have been reported to the state. Northgate Mutual reimburses approved CE course fees up to $400 per calendar year. Requests for reimbursement must be submitted through the Training Reimbursement Form (Form TR-1) within 60 days of course completion.

Field observation is required for all new auto adjusters. During the first 90 days, new adjusters must complete at least three ride-alongs with a senior adjuster and one office-based file review with their supervisor. The ride-along log (Form RO-2) must be signed by the senior adjuster and turned in to the Claims Academy coordinator.

## Chapter 2: Claim Intake

### 2.1 Overview

Claim intake is the first point of contact between Northgate Mutual and the insured or claimant. The quality of the intake interview directly affects the speed and accuracy of the entire claim lifecycle. This chapter covers how to log new claims, what information must be collected, and how to handle initial documentation requirements.

Intake is handled by the Claims Intake Unit (CIU) for personal auto policies. Commercial auto claims are handled by the Commercial Claims Unit and follow a separate intake protocol (see Chapter 11, Special Situations). The procedures in this chapter apply to personal auto claims unless otherwise noted.

### 2.2 Receiving the Claim

Claims may be reported through any of the following channels:

- Phone (toll-free claims line)
- Online through the Northgate Mutual customer portal
- Mobile app
- Fax (for paper forms from agents or body shops)
- Mail (rare; used mainly for claims submitted by attorneys)
- In person at a Northgate Mutual branch office

All reported claims must be entered into the Claims Management System (CMS) within two business hours of receipt. Claims reported after 5:00 PM local time may be entered the next business day, but the date and time of the original report must be recorded in the "Reported Date/Time" field.

When a claim is received by phone, the intake representative must verify the identity of the caller before discussing any policy information. Verification is done by asking for the policy number, the insured's name and date of birth, or the last four digits of the insured's Social Security number. If the caller cannot verify their identity, the representative must not discuss policy details and must transfer the call to the Claims Security team.

### 2.3 Initial Claim Logging

Every new claim must be logged in CMS using the New Claim screen. The following fields are required before the claim can be saved:

- Policy number
- Insured name
- Date of loss
- Time of loss (if known)
- Loss address or nearest intersection
- Cause of loss (from the drop-down list)
- Reported date and time
- Reporting party name and contact information
- Claimant name (if different from insured)
- Claimant contact information (if known)
- Description of loss (brief, 2-3 sentences)
- Vehicle information for all involved vehicles (year, make, model, VIN if available)
- Police report number (if a report was taken)
### 2.4 Coverage Determination

Before any loss investigation can begin, the assigned adjuster must confirm whether the loss is potentially covered under the policy. This step is called coverage determination. It is a written analysis, not a verbal opinion. The adjuster must document the reasoning in the Coverage Determination Worksheet (Form CDW-1) and attach it to the claim file in CMS.

The coverage determination must be completed within two business days of assignment for most claims. For claims involving a fatality, a coverage dispute, or a potential bad-faith exposure, the determination must be reviewed by a Claims Supervisor before any denial or reservation of rights letter is issued.

**Four elements must be verified:**

1.  **The policy was in force on the date of loss.** Check the declarations page and the CMS policy database. A policy that lapsed for nonpayment is not in force unless reinstatement was processed before the loss date. A policy that was cancelled for fraud is not in force. A policy that was cancelled at the insured's request is not in force.
2.  **The vehicle involved is a covered auto.** The VIN on the loss report must match the VIN listed on the declarations page. If the vehicle was newly purchased and the insured has not yet reported it, the policy may provide automatic coverage for a limited period. See Section 2.5 below for the specific rules on newly acquired autos.
3.  **The cause of loss is a covered peril.** Personal auto policies cover collision, comprehensive (fire, theft, vandalism, weather, animal strike), and liability. They do not cover mechanical breakdown, wear and tear, or damage caused by intentional acts of the insured. They do not cover damage to a vehicle that is being used for livery or rideshare unless the insured has purchased the appropriate endorsement.
4.  **The use of the vehicle at the time of loss is permitted.** The policy covers the named insured, and any family member, for personal use of the covered auto. It also covers a person using the auto with the reasonable belief that they are entitled to do so. It does not cover a person who steals the vehicle, or a person who uses the vehicle for an excluded business purpose.

**Common coverage scenarios are summarized in the table below. This table is for training purposes only. The policy language, not this table, controls.**

| Scenario | Coverage Status | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Insured rear-ends another car at a stoplight. | Covered under Part A (Liability). | Bodily injury and property damage to the other car are covered, subject to policy limits. |
| Insured's parked car is hit by a hit-and-run driver. | Covered under Part D (Collision) if the insured carries collision coverage. | If the insured does not carry collision, there is no coverage for the damage to their own car. Uninsured motorist property damage may apply in some states. |
| Insured's car is stolen and recovered with a shattered window. | Covered under Part D (Other Than Collision / Comprehensive). | Subject to the comprehensive deductible. |
| Insured's engine seizes on the highway due to low oil. | Not covered. | Mechanical breakdown is excluded. |
| Insured uses personal car to deliver pizzas for a local restaurant, without a commercial endorsement, and hits a pedestrian. | Not covered for the delivery use. | The liability exclusion for "business use" applies. The claim would be denied under the policy, and a reservation of rights letter would be issued. |
| Insured lends car to a neighbor to run an errand. Neighbor crashes. | Covered under Part A (Liability). | The neighbor is a permissive user. Coverage follows the car, subject to policy limits. |
| Insured's spouse (listed on the policy) drives the car and has an at-fault accident. | Covered under Part A (Liability). | Spouse is a family member. |
| Insured's car is damaged by a falling tree branch during a windstorm. | Covered under Part D (Other Than Collision). | Subject to the comprehensive deductible. |
| Insured's car is damaged when they intentionally back into a fence in a dispute with a neighbor. | Not covered. | Intentional act exclusion. |
SECTION 7 – CLAIM FILE DOCUMENTATION AND RECORDKEEPING

**7.1 Purpose of This Section**

A claim file is the single source of truth for every decision made on a claim. It must tell the complete story of the claim from first notice of loss through closing, in a way that another adjuster, a supervisor, or an auditor can follow without having to ask you what happened and why. If it is not in the file, it did not happen. This section covers what to put in the file, how to organize it, and how to keep it in compliance with state regulations and company policy.

**7.2 The Four C's of Claim File Documentation**

Every entry you make in a claim file should meet the Four C's:

1.  **Clear** – Write so that someone with no prior knowledge of the claim can understand the entry. Avoid vague phrases like "spoke with insured" or "reviewed file." Instead, write "Spoke with insured Jane Doe regarding estimate for rear bumper damage; she confirms she will use our preferred shop."
2.  **Concise** – Include all necessary facts, but do not pad the file with irrelevant detail. A good entry answers who, what, when, where, why, and how as applicable to the action taken.
3.  **Complete** – Capture all relevant information from every conversation, including dates, times, names of parties spoken to, and the substance of the discussion. Include your own reasoning for decisions made.
4.  **Contemporary** – Make entries promptly after the action is taken. A file that is updated in real time is more accurate and more credible than one that is back-filled days or weeks later. Do not rely on memory.

**7.3 What Must Be in Every Claim File**

The following items are required in every claim file, regardless of line of business or claim complexity. This list is not exhaustive; your supervisor may require additional documentation based on the specifics of the claim.

- **First Notice of Loss (FNOL)** information, including the date and time the claim was reported, the reporting party's name and contact information, and the initial description of the loss.
- **Policy information** relevant to the claim, including the policy number, effective dates, coverages in force, and any applicable endorsements or exclusions.
- **Coverage analysis**, including a clear statement of whether coverage applies, is denied, or is being investigated under a reservation of rights. Include the specific policy language that supports your decision.
- **All correspondence** sent to or received from the insured, claimants, attorneys, medical providers, repair facilities, and any other third parties. This includes letters, emails, and notes of phone conversations.
- **Statements** taken from the insured, claimant, witnesses, and any other involved parties. Statements may be recorded, written, or documented in a detailed diary note.
- **Photos, diagrams, and other evidence** related to the loss, including a description of what each item shows and when it was obtained.
- **Estimates and repair bills** for property damage, including any supplements or revisions.
- **Medical records and bills** for bodily injury claims, including authorizations for release of information.
- **Police reports and other official documents** related to the loss.
- **A complete diary** of all activities on the claim, including the date of each activity, what was done, and what the next step is.
- **A clear record of all payments** made on the claim, including the payee, the amount, the date, and the coverage part under which the payment was made.
- **The closing summary**, which recaps the claim, the payments made, and the reason for closing.

**7.4 Organizing the File**

A well-organized file is easy to navigate. Use the standard file organization outlined below. If you are working in a paperless environment, use the same categories as your electronic folders or tabs.

1.  **Correspondence** – All letters and emails sent and received, in chronological order (oldest to newest).
2.  **Statements** – All recorded, written, and documented statements, in chronological order.
3.  **Medical** – Medical records, bills, liens, and related correspondence, in chronological order.
4.  **Property Damage** – Estimates, repair bills, photos, and related documents, in chronological order.
5.  **Miscellaneous** – Police reports, diagrams, notes, and any other documents that do not fit in the categories above.
6.  **Diary Notes** – A running log of all claim activity. Diary notes are often kept separate from the correspondence file and are the primary place where you record your own actions and reasoning.

**Claims Academy Budget Proposal – Fiscal Year 2025**
**Submission to the Resource Allocation Committee**
**Owner: Claims Academy, Learning & Development Division**
**Submitted: 2024-09-30**
**Review Cycle: Annual Submission / Quarterly Review**

---

### 1. Executive Summary

The Claims Academy respectfully requests a total of $412,500 for Fiscal Year 2025 to support claims handling training initiatives. This request represents a 6.2% increase over the FY2024 approved budget of $388,200, driven primarily by two factors: (1) the scheduled refresh of our core claims adjuster curriculum to align with the new state regulatory requirements effective July 2025, and (2) the replacement of our aging learning management system (LMS) interface module.

The proposed allocation covers staffing, technology upgrades, external training costs, and materials/supplies. Detailed line-item justifications are provided in Section 3. The projected return on investment, including reduced claims processing error rates and improved cycle times, is summarized in Section 5.

---

### 2. Staffing Needs

The Academy's training team currently consists of 8 full-time trainers, 2 senior curriculum developers, and 1 training coordinator. We are requesting funding for one additional trainer position to handle the increased class volume expected during the Q3 regulatory rollout.

**2.1 Proposed New Position: Claims Trainer (Full-Time)**

- **Position Title:** Claims Trainer
- **Reports To:** Jennifer Alvarez supervises Claims Trainer Record status: current. (current, per HR organization chart)
- **FTE:** 1.0
- **Salary + Benefits Estimate:** $92,000
- **Start Date:** January 6, 2025 (pending approval)

**Justification:** The FY2025 training calendar includes 14 new course sections (up from 11 in FY2024) to accommodate the regulatory curriculum refresh. Without an additional trainer, we would need to either reduce course frequency or rely on overtime, which historically increases trainer burnout and reduces course evaluation scores. The new hire will be onboarded during Q1 and will shadow senior trainers for the first two months before leading independent sessions in March.

**2.2 Training Coordinator Overtime**

- **Requested Amount:** $4,500
- **Justification:** The coordinator role has absorbed scheduling and reporting duties that expanded after the LMS transition in FY2023. Overtime is requested for the Q2–Q3 peak registration period. This is a temporary measure; we will evaluate whether a permanent part-time administrative role is needed in the FY2026 cycle.

---

### 3. Line-Item Budget Categories

| **Category** | **FY2024 Approved** | **FY2025 Requested** | **Change** | **Notes** |
|--------------|---------------------|----------------------|------------|-----------|
| Staffing (salaries, benefits, overtime) | $210,000 | $306,500 | +$96,500 | Includes new trainer position and coordinator overtime |
| Technology Upgrades | $95,200 | $78,000 | -$17,200 | LMS interface module replacement; reduced scope vs. prior estimate |
| External Training Costs | $48,000 | $22,000 | -$26,000 | Vendor contracts renegotiated; fewer external certifications needed |
| Materials and Supplies | $35,000 | $6,000 | -$29,000 | Bulk printing moved in-house; digital manuals adopted |
| **Total** | **$388,200** | **$412,500** | **+$24,300** | |

*Note: The FY2024 approved figures reflect the final allocation after the mid-year adjustment in Q3 2023. The original FY2024 submission requested $410,000 but was reduced during committee review.*

---

### 4. Technology Upgrades

**4.1 LMS Interface Module Replacement – $78,000**

The current LMS interface module (installed FY2021) has reached end-of-life support from the vendor. We have experienced intermittent login failures and slow course-loading times, particularly during the 8:00 AM–10:00 AM peak usage window. Help desk tickets related to the LMS increased by 34% in Q2 2024 compared to the same period in 2023.

The $78,000 request covers:
- Software licensing and implementation: $52,000
- Data migration and testing: $18,000
- User acceptance testing and trainer familiarization: $8,000
**4.2 LMS Interface Module Replacement – Implementation Timeline and Risk Mitigation**

The implementation is scheduled for the Q3 2025 window (July–September), which avoids the peak spring certification season. The vendor has committed to a 14-week rollout, with the first 6 weeks dedicated to environment setup and configuration. We will maintain the current system in parallel for the first 4 weeks of user acceptance testing to ensure data integrity and minimize disruption.

Key risks and mitigations:

- **Data migration errors:** We are allocating 2 additional weeks of contingency in the project plan. The migration team will run three full validation passes before cutover, and we will retain a full backup of the legacy data for 90 days post-launch.
- **Trainer adoption:** The $8,000 allocated for trainer familiarization includes two half-day workshops for all eight internal trainers. We learned from the FY2023 LMS transition that early hands-on access reduced help desk calls by roughly 40% in the first month.
- **Vendor dependency:** The contract includes a service-level agreement with a 4-hour response time for critical issues during the first 30 days post-launch. After that, standard support terms apply.

We considered a lower-cost option – patching the existing module – but the vendor confirmed that end-of-life support ends December 2024. Patching would only delay the inevitable and would not resolve the underlying performance issues. The $78,000 request is the minimum viable investment to stabilize the system through FY2026.

**4.3 Deferred Technology Items – Not Requested This Cycle**

The following items were identified during our FY2025 planning but are intentionally deferred to the FY2026 cycle:

| **Item** | **Estimated Cost** | **Deferral Reason** |
|----------|-------------------|---------------------|
| Learning analytics dashboard upgrade | $45,000 | Current reporting meets regulatory requirements; upgrade is nice-to-have |
| Mobile app refresh (iOS/Android) | $28,000 | User adoption of current app is stable; revisit after LMS migration |
| Virtual reality claims simulation lab | $120,000 | Pilot program incomplete; results will inform FY2026 request |

These deferrals allow us to redirect funds to the LMS replacement, which has a more immediate impact on daily operations.

---

### 5. External Training Costs

**5.1 Vendor-Led Certification Courses – $14,000**

We have renegotiated our contract with the primary external training vendor, resulting in a 35% reduction in per-seat pricing. The $14,000 covers:

- 10 seats for the Advanced Claims Investigation certification (5-day course): $8,000
- 6 seats for the Insurance Fraud Detection workshop (2-day course): $3,600
- 4 seats for the Customer Service Excellence seminar (1-day course): $2,400

These certifications are required for staff who handle complex commercial claims and for those in the newly created senior adjuster track. The FY2024 allocation for external certifications was $26,000; the reduction reflects both the renegotiated rates and a shift toward internal training for foundational skills.

**5.2 Professional Association Memberships and Conference Fees – $5,000**

- 2 registrations for the National Association of Insurance Adjusters annual conference: $3,200
- 1 registration for the Regional Claims Leadership Summit: $900
- Annual membership renewals for 12 staff members: $900

Conference attendance is limited to senior staff who will present on our internal training model. This is a deliberate reduction from FY2024, when we sent 5 staff members to the national conference. We have determined that the ROI is higher when attendees return with structured action plans, which we will require this year.

**5.3 External Training – Not Requested**

We are not requesting funds for the following external training items this cycle:

- Leadership development program for new supervisors – deferred to FY2026, pending internal curriculum development
- Spanish-language claims handling course – being developed in-house by our bilingual staff; estimated savings of $6,000
- Advanced Excel and data analysis training – moved to a train-the-trainer model using existing staff expertise

The Claims Academy is not a physical building. It operates as a virtual training organization. All course materials, including this manual, are available on the company intranet under the Claims Training portal. Instructors are senior adjusters and managers who have completed the Trainer Certification course. If you have questions about a procedure in this manual, you should first consult your direct supervisor. If your supervisor is unable to answer, you may submit a question through the Claims Academy Help Desk.

1.2 Who Should Use This Manual

This manual is intended for all claims employees, including:

- Trainee adjusters who have completed their first week of orientation.
- Experienced adjusters who are moving into a new line of business (for example, from auto to property).
- Claims assistants and intake specialists who handle the initial report of loss.
- Supervisors and managers who are responsible for reviewing claim files for quality and compliance.
- Any employee who is new to Northgate Mutual and needs an overview of how the Claims Division operates.

If you are a trainee, you will receive a printed copy of this manual during your first day of training. You are expected to bring it to all classroom sessions and to your field training assignments. You will also have access to the electronic version, which is updated more frequently than the printed copy. The electronic version is the authoritative source. If there is a conflict between the printed manual and the electronic version, the electronic version controls.

1.3 How to Use This Manual

Each section of this manual covers one phase of the claim handling lifecycle. Sections are numbered and are designed to be read in order during your first two weeks of training. After that, you will use the manual as a reference tool. Cross-references to other sections are provided throughout. For example, when you are working on coverage determination, you will be directed to Section 4 for detailed guidelines and to Form C-101 for the coverage analysis worksheet.

At the end of most sections, you will find a list of related forms and a brief description of when each form is used. You are not expected to memorize every form number. Instead, you should become familiar with the Forms Index in Section 12 and learn to look up forms as needed.

The manual also contains a number of "Practice Pointers" that appear in shaded boxes. These are tips from experienced adjusters that are meant to help you avoid common mistakes. They are not formal policy, but they reflect the best practices that have been developed over years of claim handling.

1.4 The Claims Handling Lifecycle: A Brief Introduction

This manual follows the lifecycle of a claim from the initial report to final resolution. The lifecycle is divided into the following phases:

1. Initial Intake – The claim is reported, and basic information is collected.
2. Coverage Determination – The policy is reviewed to determine whether the loss is covered.
3. Investigation – Facts are gathered to establish liability and damages.
4. Evaluation – The claim is valued, and a settlement offer is considered.
5. Resolution – The claim is settled, denied, or litigated.

Not every claim goes through every phase in a straight line. For example, a claim may be reported, investigated, and then returned to coverage review when new facts emerge. You will learn to manage these changes as you gain experience. The important thing is to understand the purpose of each phase and the documentation that is required at each step.

1.5 The Role of the Claims Adjuster

As a claims adjuster, you are the face of Northgate Mutual to the policyholder and the claimant. Your job is to investigate the facts, apply the policy language, and make a fair and timely decision. You are also responsible for documenting your work so that another adjuster, a supervisor, or a court can understand what you did and why.

Good claim handling is built on three pillars:

- Timeliness – You must complete each step within the timeframes described in this manual and in your state's regulations.
- Accuracy – You must collect and record accurate information. Do not guess or assume. If you are unsure about a fact, ask.
- Fairness – You must treat every party with respect and make decisions based on the policy and the law, not on emotion or bias.

Course Number: A-204
Course Title: Advanced Auto Claims Handling
Course Length: 3 days (24 classroom hours)
Delivery: Instructor-led, in person at the Northgate Claims Academy training center; one session offered each quarter. A virtual option is available for adjusters located more than 100 miles from a training center.
Prerequisites: Successful completion of A-101 (Auto Claims Fundamentals) and A-102 (Property Damage Estimating) within the past 24 months. Adjusters with more than five years of continuous auto claim handling experience may request a waiver of the prerequisites from the Academy coordinator. Waiver requests must be submitted in writing and approved before registration.
Intended Audience: Claims adjusters, senior claim representatives, and claim examiners who handle auto claims involving complex coverage questions, multiple parties, or significant exposure. The course is also recommended for adjusters who are preparing for a promotion to a senior or examiner role.

Course Description

Advanced Auto Claims Handling is designed for adjusters who have mastered the fundamentals and now face the kinds of claims that do not fit neatly into the standard workflow. The course covers the following topics:

- Advanced coverage analysis, including the application of policy exclusions and endorsements in multi-vehicle accidents
- Handling claims involving uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage, including the coordination of benefits when more than one policy applies
- Investigation techniques for claims involving disputed liability, including the use of scene reconstruction reports and expert witnesses
- Evaluation of total loss vehicles, including the use of market valuation reports and the handling of diminished value claims
- Negotiation and settlement strategies for claims with multiple claimants or with claimants who are represented by counsel
- Documentation and file organization requirements for litigated claims

The course combines lecture, case study discussion, and small-group exercises. You will be asked to work through several realistic claim scenarios from initial intake to final resolution. The scenarios are based on actual claims handled by Northgate Mutual adjusters, with names and identifying details changed.

New adjusters must complete CA-101 through CA-103 before handling intake calls or entering new claims into the system. CA-104 through CA-107 must be completed within the first six months of employment. Adjusters who do not complete the Core Curriculum within the required timeframe will have their claim assignment authority suspended until the courses are finished.

Annual continuing education (CE) requirements are set by each state where the adjuster is licensed. The Licensing and Compliance team tracks CE deadlines and will notify adjusters 90 days before any license renewal date. It is the adjuster's responsibility to confirm that CE credits have been reported to the state. Northgate Mutual reimburses approved CE course fees up to $400 per calendar year. Requests for reimbursement must be submitted through the Training Reimbursement Form (Form TR-1) within 60 days of course completion.

Field observation is required for all new auto adjusters. During the first 90 days, new adjusters must complete at least three ride-alongs with a senior adjuster and one office-based file review with their supervisor. The ride-along log (Form RO-2) must be signed by the senior adjuster and turned in to the Claims Academy coordinator.

## Chapter 2: Claim Intake

### 2.1 Overview

Claim intake is the first point of contact between Northgate Mutual and the insured or claimant. The quality of the intake interview directly affects the speed and accuracy of the entire claim lifecycle. This chapter covers how to log new claims, what information must be collected, and how to handle initial documentation requirements.

Intake is handled by the Claims Intake Unit (CIU) for personal auto policies. Commercial auto claims are handled by the Commercial Claims Unit and follow a separate intake protocol (see Chapter 11, Special Situations). The procedures in this chapter apply to personal auto claims unless otherwise noted.

### 2.2 Receiving the Claim

Claims may be reported through any of the following channels:

- Phone (toll-free claims line)
- Online through the Northgate Mutual customer portal
- Mobile app
- Fax (for paper forms from agents or body shops)
- Mail (rare; used mainly for claims submitted by attorneys)
- In person at a Northgate Mutual branch office

All reported claims must be entered into the Claims Management System (CMS) within two business hours of receipt. Claims reported after 5:00 PM local time may be entered the next business day, but the date and time of the original report must be recorded in the "Reported Date/Time" field.

When a claim is received by phone, the intake representative must verify the identity of the caller before discussing any policy information. Verification is done by asking for the policy number, the insured's name and date of birth, or the last four digits of the insured's Social Security number. If the caller cannot verify their identity, the representative must not discuss policy details and must transfer the call to the Claims Security team.

### 2.3 Initial Claim Logging

Every new claim must be logged in CMS using the New Claim screen. The following fields are required before the claim can be saved:

- Policy number
- Insured name
- Date of loss
- Time of loss (if known)
- Loss address or nearest intersection
- Cause of loss (from the drop-down list)
- Reported date and time
- Reporting party name and contact information
- Claimant name (if different from insured)
- Claimant contact information (if known)
- Description of loss (brief, 2-3 sentences)
- Vehicle information for all involved vehicles (year, make, model, VIN if available)
- Police report number (if a report was taken)

documents.content:
### 2.4 Coverage Determination

Before any loss investigation can begin, the assigned adjuster must confirm whether the loss is potentially covered under the policy. This step is called coverage determination. It is a written analysis, not a verbal opinion. The adjuster must document the reasoning in the Coverage Determination Worksheet (Form CDW-1) and attach it to the claim file in CMS.

The coverage determination must be completed within two business days of assignment for most claims. For claims involving a fatality, a coverage dispute, or a potential bad-faith exposure, the determination must be reviewed by a Claims Supervisor before any denial or reservation of rights letter is issued.

**Four elements must be verified:**

1.  **The policy was in force on the date of loss.** Check the declarations page and the CMS policy database. A policy that lapsed for nonpayment is not in force unless reinstatement was processed before the loss date. A policy that was cancelled for fraud is not in force. A policy that was cancelled at the insured's request is not in force.
2.  **The vehicle involved is a covered auto.** The VIN on the loss report must match the VIN listed on the declarations page. If the vehicle was newly purchased and the insured has not yet reported it, the policy may provide automatic coverage for a limited period. See Section 2.5 below for the specific rules on newly acquired autos.
3.  **The cause of loss is a covered peril.** Personal auto policies cover collision, comprehensive (fire, theft, vandalism, weather, animal strike), and liability. They do not cover mechanical breakdown, wear and tear, or damage caused by intentional acts of the insured. They do not cover damage to a vehicle that is being used for livery or rideshare unless the insured has purchased the appropriate endorsement.
4.  **The use of the vehicle at the time of loss is permitted.** The policy covers the named insured, and any family member, for personal use of the covered auto. It also covers a person using the auto with the reasonable belief that they are entitled to do so. It does not cover a person who steals the vehicle, or a person who uses the vehicle for an excluded business purpose.

**Common coverage scenarios are summarized in the table below. This table is for training purposes only. The policy language, not this table, controls.**

| Scenario | Coverage Status | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Insured rear-ends another car at a stoplight. | Covered under Part A (Liability). | Bodily injury and property damage to the other car are covered, subject to policy limits. |
| Insured's parked car is hit by a hit-and-run driver. | Covered under Part D (Collision) if the insured carries collision coverage. | If the insured does not carry collision, there is no coverage for the damage to their own car. Uninsured motorist property damage may apply in some states. |
| Insured's car is stolen and recovered with a shattered window. | Covered under Part D (Other Than Collision / Comprehensive). | Subject to the comprehensive deductible. |
| Insured's engine seizes on the highway due to low oil. | Not covered. | Mechanical breakdown is excluded. |
| Insured uses personal car to deliver pizzas for a local restaurant, without a commercial endorsement, and hits a pedestrian. | Not covered for the delivery use. | The liability exclusion for "business use" applies. The claim would be denied under the policy, and a reservation of rights letter would be issued. |
| Insured lends car to a neighbor to run an errand. Neighbor crashes. | Covered under Part A (Liability). | The neighbor is a permissive user. Coverage follows the car, subject to policy limits. |
| Insured's spouse (listed on the policy) drives the car and has an at-fault accident. | Covered under Part A (Liability). | Spouse is a family member. |
| Insured's car is damaged by a falling tree branch during a windstorm. | Covered under Part D (Other Than Collision). | Subject to the comprehensive deductible. |
| Insured's car is damaged when they intentionally back into a fence in a dispute with a neighbor. | Not covered. | Intentional act exclusion. |

SECTION 7 – CLAIM FILE DOCUMENTATION AND RECORDKEEPING

**7.1 Purpose of This Section**

A claim file is the single source of truth for every decision made on a claim. It must tell the complete story of the claim from first notice of loss through closing, in a way that another adjuster, a supervisor, or an auditor can follow without having to ask you what happened and why. If it is not in the file, it did not happen. This section covers what to put in the file, how to organize it, and how to keep it in compliance with state regulations and company policy.

**7.2 The Four C's of Claim File Documentation**

Every entry you make in a claim file should meet the Four C's:

1.  **Clear** – Write so that someone with no prior knowledge of the claim can understand the entry. Avoid vague phrases like "spoke with insured" or "reviewed file." Instead, write "Spoke with insured Jane Doe regarding estimate for rear bumper damage; she confirms she will use our preferred shop."
2.  **Concise** – Include all necessary facts, but do not pad the file with irrelevant detail. A good entry answers who, what, when, where, why, and how as applicable to the action taken.
3.  **Complete** – Capture all relevant information from every conversation, including dates, times, names of parties spoken to, and the substance of the discussion. Include your own reasoning for decisions made.
4.  **Contemporary** – Make entries promptly after the action is taken. A file that is updated in real time is more accurate and more credible than one that is back-filled days or weeks later. Do not rely on memory.

**7.3 What Must Be in Every Claim File**

The following items are required in every claim file, regardless of line of business or claim complexity. This list is not exhaustive; your supervisor may require additional documentation based on the specifics of the claim.

- **First Notice of Loss (FNOL)** information, including the date and time the claim was reported, the reporting party's name and contact information, and the initial description of the loss.
- **Policy information** relevant to the claim, including the policy number, effective dates, coverages in force, and any applicable endorsements or exclusions.
- **Coverage analysis**, including a clear statement of whether coverage applies, is denied, or is being investigated under a reservation of rights. Include the specific policy language that supports your decision.
- **All correspondence** sent to or received from the insured, claimants, attorneys, medical providers, repair facilities, and any other third parties. This includes letters, emails, and notes of phone conversations.
- **Statements** taken from the insured, claimant, witnesses, and any other involved parties. Statements may be recorded, written, or documented in a detailed diary note.
- **Photos, diagrams, and other evidence** related to the loss, including a description of what each item shows and when it was obtained.
- **Estimates and repair bills** for property damage, including any supplements or revisions.
- **Medical records and bills** for bodily injury claims, including authorizations for release of information.
- **Police reports and other official documents** related to the loss.
- **A complete diary** of all activities on the claim, including the date of each activity, what was done, and what the next step is.
- **A clear record of all payments** made on the claim, including the payee, the amount, the date, and the coverage part under which the payment was made.
- **The closing summary**, which recaps the claim, the payments made, and the reason for closing.

**7.4 Organizing the File**

A well-organized file is easy to navigate. Use the standard file organization outlined below. If you are working in a paperless environment, use the same categories as your electronic folders or tabs.

1.  **Correspondence** – All letters and emails sent and received, in chronological order (oldest to newest).
2.  **Statements** – All recorded, written, and documented statements, in chronological order.
3.  **Medical** – Medical records, bills, liens, and related correspondence, in chronological order.
4.  **Property Damage** – Estimates, repair bills, photos, and related documents, in chronological order.
5.  **Miscellaneous** – Police reports, diagrams, notes, and any other documents that do not fit in the categories above.
6.  **Diary Notes** – A running log of all claim activity. Diary notes are often kept separate from the correspondence file and are the primary place where you record your own actions and reasoning.

**Claims Academy Budget Proposal – Fiscal Year 2025**
**Submission to the Resource Allocation Committee**
**Owner: Claims Academy, Learning & Development Division**
**Submitted: 2024-09-30**
**Review Cycle: Annual Submission / Quarterly Review**

---

### 1. Executive Summary

The Claims Academy respectfully requests a total of $412,500 for Fiscal Year 2025 to support claims handling training initiatives. This request represents a 6.2% increase over the FY2024 approved budget of $388,200, driven primarily by two factors: (1) the scheduled refresh of our core claims adjuster curriculum to align with the new state regulatory requirements effective July 2025, and (2) the replacement of our aging learning management system (LMS) interface module.

The proposed allocation covers staffing, technology upgrades, external training costs, and materials/supplies. Detailed line-item justifications are provided in Section 3. The projected return on investment, including reduced claims processing error rates and improved cycle times, is summarized in Section 5.

---

### 2. Staffing Needs

The Academy's training team currently consists of 8 full-time trainers, 2 senior curriculum developers, and 1 training coordinator. We are requesting funding for one additional trainer position to handle the increased class volume expected during the Q3 regulatory rollout.

**2.1 Proposed New Position: Claims Trainer (Full-Time)**

- **Position Title:** Claims Trainer
- **Reports To:** Jennifer Alvarez supervises Claims Trainer Record status: current. (current, per HR organization chart)
- **FTE:** 1.0
- **Salary + Benefits Estimate:** $92,000
- **Start Date:** January 6, 2025 (pending approval)

**Justification:** The FY2025 training calendar includes 14 new course sections (up from 11 in FY2024) to accommodate the regulatory curriculum refresh. Without an additional trainer, we would need to either reduce course frequency or rely on overtime, which historically increases trainer burnout and reduces course evaluation scores. The new hire will be onboarded during Q1 and will shadow senior trainers for the first two months before leading independent sessions in March.

**2.2 Training Coordinator Overtime**

- **Requested Amount:** $4,500
- **Justification:** The coordinator role has absorbed scheduling and reporting duties that expanded after the LMS transition in FY2023. Overtime is requested for the Q2–Q3 peak registration period. This is a temporary measure; we will evaluate whether a permanent part-time administrative role is needed in the FY2026 cycle.

---

### 3. Line-Item Budget Categories

| **Category** | **FY2024 Approved** | **FY2025 Requested** | **Change** | **Notes** |
|--------------|---------------------|----------------------|------------|-----------|
| Staffing (salaries, benefits, overtime) | $210,000 | $306,500 | +$96,500 | Includes new trainer position and coordinator overtime |
| Technology Upgrades | $95,200 | $78,000 | -$17,200 | LMS interface module replacement; reduced scope vs. prior estimate |
| External Training Costs | $48,000 | $22,000 | -$26,000 | Vendor contracts renegotiated; fewer external certifications needed |
| Materials and Supplies | $35,000 | $6,000 | -$29,000 | Bulk printing moved in-house; digital manuals adopted |
| **Total** | **$388,200** | **$412,500** | **+$24,300** | |

*Note: The FY2024 approved figures reflect the final allocation after the mid-year adjustment in Q3 2023. The original FY2024 submission requested $410,000 but was reduced during committee review.*

---

### 4. Technology Upgrades

**4.1 LMS Interface Module Replacement – $78,000**

The current LMS interface module (installed FY2021) has reached end-of-life support from the vendor. We have experienced intermittent login failures and slow course-loading times, particularly during the 8:00 AM–10:00 AM peak usage window. Help desk tickets related to the LMS increased by 34% in Q2 2024 compared to the same period in 2023.

The $78,000 request covers:
- Software licensing and implementation: $52,000
- Data migration and testing: $18,000
- User acceptance testing and trainer familiarization: $8,000

**4.2 LMS Interface Module Replacement – Implementation Timeline and Risk Mitigation**

The implementation is scheduled for the Q3 2025 window (July–September), which avoids the peak spring certification season. The vendor has committed to a 14-week rollout, with the first 6 weeks dedicated to environment setup and configuration. We will maintain the current system in parallel for the first 4 weeks of user acceptance testing to ensure data integrity and minimize disruption.

Key risks and mitigations:

- **Data migration errors:** We are allocating 2 additional weeks of contingency in the project plan. The migration team will run three full validation passes before cutover, and we will retain a full backup of the legacy data for 90 days post-launch.
- **Trainer adoption:** The $8,000 allocated for trainer familiarization includes two half-day workshops for all eight internal trainers. We learned from the FY2023 LMS transition that early hands-on access reduced help desk calls by roughly 40% in the first month.
- **Vendor dependency:** The contract includes a service-level agreement with a 4-hour response time for critical issues during the first 30 days post-launch. After that, standard support terms apply.

We considered a lower-cost option – patching the existing module – but the vendor confirmed that end-of-life support ends December 2024. Patching would only delay the inevitable and would not resolve the underlying performance issues. The $78,000 request is the minimum viable investment to stabilize the system through FY2026.

**4.3 Deferred Technology Items – Not Requested This Cycle**

The following items were identified during our FY2025 planning but are intentionally deferred to the FY2026 cycle:

| **Item** | **Estimated Cost** | **Deferral Reason** |
|----------|-------------------|---------------------|
| Learning analytics dashboard upgrade | $45,000 | Current reporting meets regulatory requirements; upgrade is nice-to-have |
| Mobile app refresh (iOS/Android) | $28,000 | User adoption of current app is stable; revisit after LMS migration |
| Virtual reality claims simulation lab | $120,000 | Pilot program incomplete; results will inform FY2026 request |

These deferrals allow us to redirect funds to the LMS replacement, which has a more immediate impact on daily operations.

---

### 5. External Training Costs

**5.1 Vendor-Led Certification Courses – $14,000**

We have renegotiated our contract with the primary external training vendor, resulting in a 35% reduction in per-seat pricing. The $14,000 covers:

- 10 seats for the Advanced Claims Investigation certification (5-day course): $8,000
- 6 seats for the Insurance Fraud Detection workshop (2-day course): $3,600
- 4 seats for the Customer Service Excellence seminar (1-day course): $2,400

These certifications are required for staff who handle complex commercial claims and for those in the newly created senior adjuster track. The FY2024 allocation for external certifications was $26,000; the reduction reflects both the renegotiated rates and a shift toward internal training for foundational skills.

**5.2 Professional Association Memberships and Conference Fees – $5,000**

- 2 registrations for the National Association of Insurance Adjusters annual conference: $3,200
- 1 registration for the Regional Claims Leadership Summit: $900
- Annual membership renewals for 12 staff members: $900

Conference attendance is limited to senior staff who will present on our internal training model. This is a deliberate reduction from FY2024, when we sent 5 staff members to the national conference. We have determined that the ROI is higher when attendees return with structured action plans, which we will require this year.

**5.3 External Training – Not Requested**

We are not requesting funds for the following external training items this cycle:

- Leadership development program for new supervisors – deferred to FY2026, pending internal curriculum development
- Spanish-language claims handling course – being developed in-house by our bilingual staff; estimated savings of $6,000
- Advanced Excel and data analysis training – moved to a train-the-trainer model using existing staff expertise
